---
title: Use cases
description: "Frame forecasting, recommendations, customer outcomes, and relational learning as concrete datasets and prediction tasks."
engine: markdown
---

Suppose you have records about customers, products, devices, or other entities,
with related events arriving over time. You want a prediction from the
information available at a particular decision: tomorrow's demand, a candidate
product's relevance, or a customer's next outcome.

RelFlow is a model factory for typed, nested data. Declare the fields,
record collections, and prediction objectives; that schema generates a custom
neural architecture for your observations. The useful starting point is the
decision and its dataset. Define what one observation contains, when its
inputs are available, and what answer will eventually be observed.

## Choose a prediction task

| Application | One observation | What to predict | Worked design |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Demand, load, or sensor forecasting | One series at a cutoff, with its observed history and requested future times | A number at each requested future time | [Time series forecasting](time-series-forecasting.qmd) |
| Product or content recommendations | One customer, candidate, and decision, with the earlier interaction history | The candidate's later click, purchase, or rating | [Recommendations](recommendations.qmd) |
| Retention and customer value | One eligible customer at a cutoff, with profile and purchase records | Inactivity or spending over a defined future window | [Customer outcomes](customer-outcomes.qmd) |
| Predictions across related tables | One scored entity or entry, with related records grouped beneath it | A later Boolean or numeric outcome | [Relational prediction](relational-prediction.qmd) |
| Reuse across tasks | One entity snapshot described by a trained model | Exported context used by a separate predictor | [Representation learning](representation-learning.qmd) |
| Payment review | One payment or account review, with the information known then | A later dispute or account loss | [The payment learning path](../learn/your-first-model.qmd) |

These pages contain illustrative model designs and the comparisons needed to
assess them. The [evidence](../evidence.qmd) contains recorded experiments on
individual mechanisms. A schema example describes a task the library can
express; its quality on an application's data still needs measurement.

## Match the structure to the decision

Start with ordinary supervised learning: a [Boolean](../datatypes/boolean.qmd)
for a yes-or-no outcome, a [Number](../datatypes/number.qmd) for a numeric
outcome, or a [Category](../datatypes/category.qmd) for a label. A flat record
is sufficient when those fields contain the evidence the decision needs.

Add a [Branch](../datatypes/branch.qmd) when individual related records matter.
An interaction can keep its item, action, and time together. A purchase can
contain line items, with further record collections nested beneath them when
the dataset calls for it. Separate histories can describe different event
types, each with its own ordering and resource limit. Targets can belong to
the whole observation or to records at different depths inside those branches.

The field names come from your dataset. Your application chooses the types,
nesting, and targets; RelFlow constructs the neural modules from those
declarations. [Model tree](../concepts/model-tree.qmd#how-declarations-become-a-model)
explains that construction. The type system is extensible: a
[custom field type](../datatypes/custom-tensorfields.qmd) can supply its own
data encoding and prediction behavior through the field protocol.

## Define the dataset before fitting

For any of these designs, make four decisions before writing the model:

1. **Observation and cutoff.** Identify the entity or candidate being scored
   and the instant at which its inputs become fixed.
2. **Available context.** Assemble the fields and related records known then,
   preserving time order, record identity, and nested relationships.
3. **Outcome and horizon.** State what the target means, when its answer is
   ready, and which observations have complete labels.
4. **Comparison.** Select the same held-out decisions for the RelFlow model
   and a useful simple baseline, then measure the application's objective.

[Prepare observations](../learn/prepare-observations.qmd) demonstrates these
choices for payments. [Data modules](../guides/data-modules.qmd) supplies the
prepared data, and [Evaluation](../learn/evaluation.qmd) connects scores to
decisions. Joins, observation construction, and split assignment belong to
the application.

## Train for one task or build for reuse

For a labeled task, train the generated model on prepared observations and
evaluate its predictions. A saved model can produce batch predictions or
serve predictions and requested representations through
[HTTP serving](../guides/serving.qmd) in your application's infrastructure.

To build a foundation model for your own structured data, begin with a
broader [reconstruction pretraining](../learn/pretraining-and-fine-tuning.qmd)
task, then adapt its objectives and fine-tune for labeled decisions, or reuse
its learned [representations](representation-learning.qmd) in separate
predictors. Schema changes retain compatible learned state under the
[mutation rules](../guides/schema-mutation.qmd). This pretraining and reuse
workflow needs evaluation for each downstream task; a newly initialized
task-specific model has not undergone it.

## Related work and demonstrated behavior

The customer and multi-table examples adapt public RelBench task formulations.
Their task definitions and adaptations are cited on those pages. The examples
show how to structure an application; they do not reproduce benchmark runs or
report rankings.

For the modeling mechanisms, inspect the recorded
[identity comparison](../evidence/identity/unseen-identity-equality.html),
[retrieval capacity](../evidence/relational/retrieval-capacity.html), and
[representation transfer](../evidence/representation/reconstruction-transfer.html)
experiments. Their results apply to their specified setups. Use the worked
designs here to formulate an application, then compare it on the data and
decision it is intended to support.
